title: 3  Substitution, Variables, and Functions
text:
3.3 What is a variable really?
Placeholders as they are used in everyday life introduce confusion with data. In contemporary US English, especially in the practice of Law, the name “John Doe” is meant as a placeholder for a yet unnamed person. If compared to other names it may not stand out as variable, which is the point, it is a name that can be used in the software and many forms that require a name while still not being attached to any specific person. In the other direction a name like “Malcom X” could place an order at Konstants as “x”, but now this is not the placeholder but the actual name. So the roles of data and variables is often quite difficult to distinguish.
The resolution is that we need to keep track of two alphabets. One alphabet is how we write down our data. The second alphabet is for variables.

To create substitution you need

An alphabet for data, whose characters we call ‘constants’.
A separate infinite alphabet for variables, whose characters we call ‘variables’.

A character from either alphabet is called a token. A list of tokens is called a string.
Along with those two alphabets we allow punctuation, spaces and parenthesis to gather symbols together in a grammar. These are not considered part of the tokens.

The role of the “infinite” in the variables alphabet will be seen when we fix the paradox. For now we can at least answer one question. A variable is not a placeholder, fill-in-the-blank, or a stand-in for data. It has instead a boring but precise answer.
What is a variable? A variable is a character from the variable alphabet.






WarningTracking Two Alphabets



Having two sorts of data is confusing and requires that we make an effort to tell everyone what we intended. In mathematics we often expect our reader to have experience and so we leave these important distinctions unsaid. For example, we often just assume you have used \(x\) as a placeholder before an you will default to using it that way now.
Programs are more forthcoming with clues about our two alphabets of data versus variables. You may need to include special markers, e.g. var x to denote the variable \(x\) and 'x' to denote the letter \(x\). Unfortunately, even programs have their ambiguity. For example, it may be as subtle as where in the grammar you use the symbol, such as def exchange(x,y): which treats the x in exchange as a letter but the x in (x,y) as a variable.
This would be a good place to mention that the term “alphabet” as used in programming would be more in line with what in English you know as a dictionary of words. So when you read “exchange” in this program you should see it as one character. To replace “exchange” we would replace the entire word, not its individual letters. This is more in line with characters in the Chinese alphabet or Egyptian hieroglyphics.
You learn these differences as the syntax and grammar of the programming language and every programming language has its own rules. Most programming languages are descendants of a few common ancestors (ALGOL, COBOL, Fortran, and Lisp). So you likely will find it gets easier to read these implied rules once you have been exposed to a few examples.



In the following code sample, find the tokens of the alphabets and identify them as either constants or variables. You are not expected to know all these languages and you may find it helpful to consult an AI code assistant for some hints.

MathALGOLCOBOLFortranLisp


\[
f(x) := \begin{cases}
    \text{Curry} & \text{if } x = \text{Haskell}\\
    \text{Curry} & \text{if } x = \text{Robert}\\
\end{cases}
\]


begin
    string procedure f(x);
    string x;
    if x = "Haskell" then
        f := "Curry"
    else if x = "Robert" then
        f := "Curry";
end


WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 X PIC X(10).
01 Y PIC X(10).

PROCEDURE DIVISION.
        EVALUATE TRUE
            WHEN X = "Haskell" OR X = "Robert"
                MOVE "Curry" TO Y
        END-EVALUATE.


character(len=10) function f(x)
character(len=*), intent(in) :: x

if (x == "Haskell" .or. x == "Robert") then
    f = "Curry"
end if

end function f


(defun f (x)
    (cond ((string= x "Haskell") "Curry")
        ((string= x "Robert") "Curry")))





How to assign a variable.
Since a variable \(x\) is a placeholder we need a method to replace it. We say that we are “assigning a value”. Many notations have been invented for this but amongst the most common is the humorously named “Walrus” symbol \(:=\) to indicate this.
\[
\begin{aligned}
(x\mapsto \text{Curry})|_{x:=\text{Haskell}} & \text{ means } \text{Haskell}\mapsto \text{Curry}\\
(x\mapsto \text{Curry})|_{x:=\text{Robert}} & \text{ means } \text{Robert}\mapsto \text{Curry}\\
& \vdots
\end{aligned}
\]
Notice the language of “assignment” is different than the language of “equality”. We are not “making \(x\) equal to ‘Haskell’”.
If we did then it would later seems strange to say “\(x\) now equals ‘Robert’; one thing cannot equal two different things. Meanwhile it seems appropriate to assign different substitutes for a variable. Programming literature often clarifies this by describing a variable as location or address in memory where data will be stored. When assignments x:="Curry" happen, the program copies the data "Curry" into the address of the variable x. This captures the spirit of the two separate alphabets as well: one for honest data, and one for location of that data. Unfortunately connecting variables to something physical like memory introduces limitations like the size of what we can store which are not part of the purely conceptual idea of a variable as a placeholder for any data.
Notation options. Despite the mistaken impression that equals notation gives to assignment, so much history is invested in this that it is impossible to avoid it in our everyday encounters with math and software. In mathematics it is common to find the same symbol \(=\) used for both equality testing and an assignment. The trick is that mathematics permits the addition of words and paragraphs explaining what particular role we intended. So we can say “If \(x=5\)…” to suggest a test of equality and “Set \(x=5\)…” to demand an assignment. In programming languages brevity and clarity are preferred so we often keep two different symbols. Some use a double equal sign == for the comparison and = for assignment. Others use words x.equals(y) or x eq y or similar syntax to literally spell out what they intend.


Curry-Feys Substitution rules
We would like to finally settle the paradox of the trapped variable. So let us imagine what it is we need to do to substitute. First we have a string \(M\) of tokens and a variable \(x\). Let us write down the rules for substitution the way we think of placeholders. The substitution rules are named after the mathematician/Computer Scientist Haskell Curry and logician Robert Feys who wrote them down in their book Combinatory Logic in 1958. The rules are precise, at times tricky, but they avoid our paradox so they are widely accepted today.

We will write \(M|_{x:=N}\) to mean “substitute \(N\) for \(x\) in \(M\)”.

Remember that “constant” just means a token in the constant alphabet and “variable” just means a token in the variable alphabet. So the rules that follow only care about the alphabet not some intuition about variables and constants. \[
\tag{Constant Rule}
c|_{x:=N}\text{ yields }c \text{ for constants }c.
\]


MathPythonJavaSwift


\(\text{Curry}|_{x:=\text{Haskell}}\) yields \(\text{Curry}\).


\(M\) has nothing to do with \(x\) so assigning \(x\) to \(N\) does not change \(M\).
M = "Curry"
x = "Haskell"
print(M)  # yields "Curry"


\(M\) has nothing to do with \(x\) so assigning \(x\) to \(N\) does not change \(M\).
String M = "Curry";
String x = "Haskell";
System.out.println(M);  // yields "Curry"


\(M\) has nothing to do with \(x\) so assigning \(x\) to \(N\) does not change \(M\).
let M = "Curry"
let x = "Haskell"
print(M)  // yields "Curry"




\[
\tag{Same Variable Rule}
x|_{x:=N}\text{ yields }N
\]


MathJavaMathematic


For example, \(x|_{x:=\text{Haskell}}\) yields \(\text{Haskell}\).


String x;
String x = "Haskell";
System.out.println(x);  // prints "Haskell"


Clear[x]
x = "Haskell"
x  (* yields "Haskell" *)




\[
\tag{Distinct Variable Rule}
y|_{x:=N}\text{ yields }y \text{ if } y\neq x.
\]


MathJavaMathematics


\(c|_{x:=N}\) yields \(c\), where \(c\) is a variable just not the variable \(x\).
For example, \(\text{Curry}|_{x:=\text{Haskell}}\) yields \(\text{Curry}\).


\(M\) has nothing to do with \(x\) so assigning \(x\) to \(N\) does not change \(M\). However, in software often you cannot have a variable without some actual data, it might just fill in a default value like \(0\) or null.
String M;
String x = "Haskell";
System.out.println(M);  // prints null 


\(M\) has nothing to do with \(x\) so assigning \(x\) to \(N\) does not change \(M\). In symbolic programming languages you can often keep \(M\) as a variable without need for a default value. This is closest to the mathematical idea.
Clear[M]
x = "Haskell"
M  (* yields M *)




\[
\tag{Repeat Rule}
(LR)|_{x:=N}\text{ yields }L|_{x:=N}R|_{x:=N}
\]


MathPythonIdris


For example, \((x+y+x)|_{x:=\text{Curry}}\) yields \(\text{Curry}+y+\text{Curry}\). You can choose \(L=x+y\) and \(R=+x\) for example. Notice \(L=x+\) and \(R=y+x\) would also work. The point is that you can break the string into two parts and substitute into each part.


The repeated use of variables in most programming languages use the same value as many times as needed.
x = "Haskell"   
M = x + x
print(M)  # prints "HaskellHaskell"


Be careful. In some modern languages like Rust and Idris you may be limited in how many times you can use a variable. Here is an example where the number 1 tell the system to use the value of x exactly once. If you try to use it more than once the program will not compile.
dupFail : (1 x : String) -> String
dupFail x = x ++ x -- Will not compile: x is used twice.
dupOk :  String -> String
dupOk x = x ++ x -- Now succeeds because x is unrestricted.




So far these are precise and somewhat the meaning of “fill-in-the-blank”. What we have not yet done is consider what to do if we try to substitute into a function!

THe rest of the rules concern substitution into \(x\mapsto M\) strings.

Lets begin with a named function \(K\) that takes an input \(x\) and returns the constant \(c\).
def K(x):
    return c
c = "Curry"

print(K("Robert"))  # prints "Curry"
If \(M\) is the program return c, then this is simply naming the lambda \(x\mapsto c\). To feed in “Curry” for \(c\) we have to assign \(c:=\text{Curry}\) which we do in line 3. So after this line we have \(x\mapsto \text{Curry}\). The last line confirmed this by inputting “Robert” for \(x\) and getting “Curry” as the output. Thus following line 3 we could think of the program as equal to this.
def K(x):
    return "Curry"

print(K("Robert"))  # prints "Curry"
This suggests the following rule. \[
\tag{Incorrect Rule}
(x\mapsto M)|_{c:=N} \text{ yields } x\mapsto (M|_{c:=N})
\] The question mark is because here comes the source of the trapped variable paradox. See if \(N=x\) we can completely change the nature of the program. \[
(x\mapsto c)|_{c:=x} \text{ yields } x\mapsto (c|_{c:=x}) \text{ yields }x\mapsto x.
\] We just turned a function \(x\mapsto c\) that is intended to be constant into one that outputs variable values. So we have to be much more careful and refuse this naive substitution.
If we really want to maintain substitution \(c:=x\) without confusing it with the \(x\) in \(x\mapsto M\) it is as if there really are two different variables both with the same name \(x\). We could just give one of these a new nickname, perhaps \(\acute{x}\) or local_x. We replace \(x\) in our program by this nickname, then we substitute. It is two step process. \[
\tag{Scope Rule}
(x\mapsto M)|_{c:=N} \text{ yields } \acute{x}\mapsto \Big(M|_{x:=\acute{x}}\Big)\Big|_{c:=N}
\]









Original
Renamed
Result




def K(x):
    return c
c = x
def K(local_x):
    return c
c = x
def K(local_x):
    return x




The point is that when we write \(x\mapsto M\) we bind \(x\) to \(M\) in such a way that this \(x\) is the private property of \(M\). We can therefore rename it to avoid confusion with later uses of \(x\) that would substantially alter the meaning of the program. We see now that the whole problem was that when give instructions and we reuse a variable outside when it is already used inside (thus trapping the variable) the inside variable should be thought of as different and given a never before used nickname like \(\acute{x}\).






WarningUnintended Consequences



The striking prediction of this rule is that we need to be able at any point to come up with a variable name that has never been used before. But variables are simply characters in our variable alphabet. So we now see why it was crucial that our variable alphabet be infinite. If we had a finite alphabet we would eventually run out of new names and be unable to rename a variable to avoid trapping it.
It is a remarkably deep and subtle point that getting substitution to work seems to require that we accept a concept as complicated as infinity. We have not even begun doing much interesting computation and already we are depending on concepts that humans have struggled with for thousands of years.


Programming languages solve the trapped variable paradox in similar ways but often introduce indentation, braces, and other notation to make it easy to identify where a variable is meant to need a nickname, so-called local variable. Other variables are called global and the discussion of local/global is known as scope. Sometimes a variable is reused many times cause there to be several levels nicknames, i.e. “scope”, such as in this program.

\[
\begin{aligned}
(x\mapsto (x\mapsto c))|_{c:=x} & \text{ yields } \dot{x}\mapsto \Big((x\mapsto c)|_{x:=\dot{x}}\Big)\Big|_{c:=x} \\
    & \text{ yields } \dot{x}\mapsto (x\mapsto c)|_{c:= x}\\
    & \text{ yields } \dot{x}\mapsto (\ddot{x}\mapsto (c|_{c:= x}))\\
    & \text{ yields } \dot{x}\mapsto (\ddot{x}\mapsto x)
\end{aligned}   
\]

Here is the same example as Python program.










Original
First Nickname
Second Nickname
Result




def K(x):
  def L(x):
      return c
  return L
c = x
def K(x_temp_1):
    c = x
    def L(x):
        return c
    return L
def K(x_temp_1):
    def L(x_temp_2):
        c = x
        return c
    return L
def K(x_temp_1):
    def L(x_temp_2):
        return x
    return L




Often the term scope is used to describe when a variable should be thought of as having a nickname that isn’t known outside of program. The terms local variable are used for variables that need nicknames and global variable for ones that can be used without a nickname. It is the job of the programming language to provide nicknames and keep track of local/global scope. However, the programs that result from these choices can offer surprising outcomes that cause many programs to seem to behave in peculiar ways. Let us look at a few.

title: 3  Substitution, Variables, and Functions
text:
3.4 Alternative: Giving up on variables
One idea to prevent the paradox of a trapped variable occurred first to Shonfinkle and explored extensively by Curry and Feys is to get ride of the use of variables entirely. Instead focus on a list of allowed operations that can be applied to data. These operations were known as combinators but most people today will know them as gates. We can explore this with some examples.

In the Konstants restaraunts, \(K\) is the combinator. When followed by two pieces of data (which can be grouped in parentheses) it yields the first of the two ignoring the second.

K "Curry" "Fries" yields "Curry".
K 3 7 yields 3.
K (3 7) 5 yields 3 7. The parentheses around (3 7) forced us to treat that as one piece of data and so it was the first of the two pieces and thus returned.
Working from the outside in, K (K 3 7) 5 yields K 3 7 (the first term to the outermost \(K\)) which in turn yields 3.
Now working from the inside-out, K (K 3 7) 5 yields K 3 5 (the second \(K\) was applied first to 3 7) which still yields 3.


Viewed form the perspective of the second term, this is a constant function.

The identity combinator \(I\) is defined by \(I~x\) yields \(x\). It simply returns its argument unchanged.

Notice there are no variables and no substitution. Just computations. In fact, we could make these two combinators as simple machines. The game now is to list a number of combinators that can assist you in building a program.
It may surprise you to learn how powerful K together with I can be. For example, the next exercise asks you to confirm that combining K and I is already enough to make a program that manages the concept of if a then b else c.

Let K be represent “True” and K I represent “False”; and define a new combinator IF by IF a b c = I a b c. Show that:

IF True 3 7 yields 3
IF False 3 7 yields 7

Because of this behavior, the IF combinator is usually called a conditional combinator and instead of IF a b c we write it:
if a then b else c

So far we chain together our combinators as lists, but once we make a clever little program like if-then-else we might want to compose it with other little programs without physically rewriting all the lines of instructions. We can do that with a combinator specially built to combine two programs into one and apply them in a specified order.

The \(S\) combinator (for Schonfinkle) is defined so that \(S~f~g~x\) yields \(f~x~(g~x)\). It allows us to apply a function to an argument and then apply another function to the same argument, combining the results.

S f g x yields f x (g x). S K K 3 yields K 3 (K 3) which in turn yields K 3 3 which finally yields 3.



Set B to be S (K S) K. Show that B f g x yields f (g x). That is, B behaves like the composition combinator, it applies the program f to the output of the program g.

When you think of the operations of combinators like K, I, and S it may strike you as highly mechanical. That is the right picture to have. And perhaps you are also convinced that in combination they begin to make a tiny bit of sophistication, such as if-then-else, counting, possibly more. Well in fact they can do everything any computer can do.l.

The S, K, I combinators together are enough to do all computations.

Notice the complete absence of substitution and variables so the trapped variable problem just does not exist in computations. Gone also is the requirement that we are secretly depending on infinity to get substitution to work. It was only ever a mistake in vague mathematics and the programming languages used to bridge humans to machines. Put another way, humans who can imagine a place for infinity are beyond what a machine can imagine for itself.

\(S~K~K~x\) yields \(x\). In this sense \(S~K~K\) behaves like the identity combinator \(I\).


Applied Combinators and modern hardware
Unfortunately it is not the case that using just these three combinators is a fast way to write practical programs. For example we saw we do not really need \(I\) because we can get the same behavior as S K K. But doing three operations instead of one is silly. Modern day CPUs therefore boast over a thousand additional instructions (applied combinators) and GPUs use a few hundred. Even so, given more time to operate, any one of these devices can compute anything that is computable. That was the insight of Alan Turing and Alonzo Church and it is known today as the Turing-Church thesis.
As another exercise you can invent counting, additions, binary numbers, decimal numbers and on and on. But those will be very slow. Instead you are better off adding many more combinators to your list to give yourself a solid start.

In the Intel x86 instruction set there is a command to add two numbers. ADD. It takes the next to terms and adds them.

ADD 3 7 yields 10.
Working from the inside-out, ADD (ADD 3 7) 5 yields ADD 10 5 which in turn yields 15.
Working from the outside in, ADD (ADD 3 7) 5 gets stuck! Based on work from the outside we have not yet computed ADD 3 7 and so the outside ADD is stuck waiting on that number before it can continue.

Notice how the ADD operation is not as straight-forward as the K and I or even the IF combinator in that ADD really only makes sense when followed by numbers. This is why it got stuck when working outside-in instead of inside-out. It is striking that something as basic as adding can run into trouble based purely on how we ask the question. To get unstuck we would need to go into the design of the hardware and rewrite the order of operations. This highlights the difference between pure combinators like \(K\) and applied combinators like ADD. This is what is known as an “Applied Combinator”.


A fixed-point combinator \(F\) is one where \(F~g\) yields \(g~(F~g)\). We call this a fixed-point because \(g\) applied to \(F~g\) yields the same result as \(F~g\) itself, so the “point” \(F~g\) is fixed. When introduced as an option for computation they give the programmer a way to have an operation applied to itself repeatedly in a process known as recursion. That is an essential power in modern programming so the ability to create such a combinator (or gate) is highly valuable. The mathematician Alanzo Church (1903-1995) found one such operator he called \(Y\) and Alan Turing (1912-1954) discovered another called \(\Theta\).

There is a tech incubator launched in 2005 called the “Y Combinator” which also hosts “Hacker News”, a website dedicated to articles and announcements on cutting edge technology.

3.5 Abstraction “Fixes” a paradox
A common feature of “fixing” a paradox is that we agree to give up on something. In this example, to give up on constants and variables is to give up a lot of the ways we have learned to talk about science. Yet to put rules on what substitution looks like, goes against the “fill-in-the-box” intuition we spent years building for ourselves.
Whenever we encounter a situation where we limit our thinking by rules we have what is called an abstraction.

An abstraction is to limit a topic by rules.

We will have many opportunities to explore abstraction within computation, but the word is so common you might benefit from some outside examples to connect your learning with what you already experience. In economics, workers do many different jobs but to make it possible to compare their productivity we can limit their jobs to how much money they earn. The money is the abstraction.

An abstract painting such as Marcel Duchamp’s Nude Descending a Staircase the nude figure is limited to having a head, arms, and legs. This allowed the subject of the abstract art to consider the locomotion of descending a staircase rather than the details of a specific person.



Nude Descending a Staircase, by Marcel Duchamp (1887-1968) - Philadelphia Museum of Art, PD-US



Possibly here is a place to imagine how data we collect for computations is typically an abstraction of whatever we want to explore. You have some control in creating abstractions when you compute. Choose your rules wisely, they will have consequences.

text:
4.1 Tarski’s Thesis
One of the giants of 20th century logic, Alfred Tarski, gave an account of “What are Logical Notions?” His answer considered how these ideas evolved in history. He gave the following thoughts.
We can do no better than to use Tarski’s own example. If our world is Euclid’s geometry, then a triangle is a shape outlined by three lines. Two triangles are congruent if they have the same angles and lengths of sides. It does not matter if we draw one of these triangles in another room, rotated, or reflected in a mirror. By abstracting to a world where triangles are their edges and their angles we give up on other things that would set them apart. So what does not change when we talk about a triangle with Euclid are topics like length and angles. Those become the logical notions of Euclidean geometry.
The brilliance of this perspective is that it allows us adjust our logic as we change our world. Already Euclid sensed this need because not everyone will use the same ruler. The ability to scale a triangle leads to giving up length as a logical notion and comparing triangles only if they are similar.
And a property even more abstract is that in a triangle three vertices are connected by three edges. All triangles share that property and it sets them apart form say squares and rectangles. That view of geometry was latter called “topology” and you see whenever you look at a map of bus routes where the stops are evenly spaced and the lines are mostly straight even though the bus no doubt takes much different times to reach tops and twists and turns on its way. After abstracting to the level of what stop comes next distance is not a logical notion.
Now the point of Tarski’s thesis was to draw the experiment to its most extreme conclusions. Imagine that you have abstracted away everything. What logical notions would remain? If you can explain those then those notions should be the foundation of all reasoning. With the right imagination you can see there is no way to forget everything but if you forget nearly everything you will start to see a few logical notions seem to remain, for example, the concepts of “and”, “or”, “not”, “if…then”, and “true” and “false”. These are the logical operators that we will explore in this book.

title: 4  Logical Operators
text:
4.2 Logical Operators: Language, Introduction, Elimination (LIE)

To create a logical operator we need to specify three things:

Language: the symbols and grammar to be used to express the logical operator.
Introduction: what we need in place to create an instance of the logical operator.
Elimination: what we need in place along with context to use a logical operator.

Throughout this book we use the acronym LIE to remember these three components of a logical operator. Allow yourself to smirk win you turn in a “LIE” as part of your homework.

The English word “AND” is a bit too generic to make a reliable logical operator. For instance, we might write

12 is positive and even
Study and you will get good grades.

In the first sentence 12 is given two properties that happen to coexist. This is the way logic thinks of “and”. Meanwhile the second sentence seems to indicate that the first property (studying) is responsible for the second (good grades). If you need further confirmation that something is different about these two uses consider swapping the order.

12 is even and positive
You will get good grades and study.

Be aware that logic steps back the options for the meaning of everyday words so that when used confusion is minimized.
In order to introduce logical operators recall from your childhood the notations used for other operators such as addition and multiplication:
\[
\begin{array}{rc}
  & 11\\
  + & 12\\
\hline
  & 23
\end{array}
\qquad
\begin{array}{rc}
  & 11\\
  * & 12\\
\hline
  & 132
\end{array}
\] We will use a similar notation to begin explaining our logical operators and later we will adjust this into what is known as “sequent calculus”.


Language: \(\wedge\) (“wedge” but pronounced “and”) is used to represent the logical operator “and”. The grammar for “and” is given by the following production rule: \[
\tag{$L_{\wedge}$}
\langle conjunction \rangle ::= \langle proposition \rangle \wedge \langle proposition \rangle
\]
Introduction: If \(P\) and \(Q\) are judged as valid then so is \(P\wedge Q\). In symbols \[
  \tag{$I_{\wedge}$}
  \begin{array}{rc}
   & P\\
  \wedge  &  Q\\
  \hline
  & P \wedge Q
  \end{array}
  \]
Elimination: If \(P\wedge Q\) is judged as valid then so are \(P\) and \(Q\). In symbols we want to remove the wedge and one side of the formula, so we think of this as subtraction type step which we denote by \(\wedge -\) to remove the right term and \(-\wedge\) to remove the left term. Worse notations have been invented, wait until you read the example from Lisp. \[
  \tag{$E_{\wedge}$}
  \begin{array}{rc}
   \wedge -   & P \wedge Q\\
  \hline
  & P
  \end{array}
  \qquad
  \begin{array}{rc}
   -\wedge   & P \wedge Q\\
  \hline
  & Q
  \end{array}
  \]


It may surprise you to notice that the LIE for AND we just used does specify what form of judgement we are using. This is the model in all logics be they Computational, Theoretical, or Practical. However, when we include those as added information we get more precise descriptions of this logical operator which we will come to later.


Language: \(\to\) (“arrow” but pronounced “implies”) is used to represent the logical operator “implies”. The grammar for “implies” is given by the following production rule: \[
\tag{$L_{\to}$}
\langle implication \rangle ::= \langle proposition \rangle \to \langle proposition \rangle
\]
Introduction: If \(P\) and \(Q\) are judged as valid then so is \(P\to Q\). In symbols \[
  \tag{$I_{\to}$}
  \begin{array}{rc}
\to   & P\vdash Q\\
  \hline
  & P \to Q
  \end{array}
  \]
Elimination: If \(P\to Q\) is judged as valid then so is \(Q\) if \(P\) is also judged as valid. In symbols \[
  \tag{$E_{\to}$}
  \begin{array}{rc}
   & P\to Q\\ @ & P   \\
  \hline
  & Q
  \end{array}
  \]



Using \(\vee\) (“vee” but pronounced “or”) as the symbol for the logical operator “or”, write down a LIE for “or”.


Language of “And”
The best tool language has for clarifying meaning is the use of a grammar. If we keep to a context-free grammar we can be certain that everyone reads the meaning the same. So here is a grammar we can give to “and” to fit our logical purposes. Note, in historical settings the term “conjunction” is often used as synonym for “and”. Using “conjunction” can often solve the annoying problem needing to use “and” as an every day word while also talking about “and” in a logical way.

In symbolic language \(\wedge\) (“wedge” but pronounced “and”) is used to represent the logical operator “and”. The grammar for “and” is given by the following production rule: \[
\tag{$L_{\wedge}$}
\langle conjunction \rangle ::= \langle proposition \rangle \wedge \langle proposition \rangle
\] In natural language we can say “A and B” where A and B are propositions. Alternatives include &, && and AND but we will stick to \(\wedge\) for the rest of this book.

Notice what we have not allowed are some the natural ways that “and” drifts in language, e.g. 

“7 is positive, odd and prime”

would now need to be said more like this:

“(7 is positive) and ((7 is odd) and (7 is prime))”

We forgive most authors who slide back to the more natural language uses of “and” but it will strengthen your understanding to practice this in a precise way for a while.

In a theoretical judgment where we forget about evidence then all we need from propositions is their truth value. We can ask for this in most programming languages by builtin logical operators that are written in a variety of ways. Here are some popular options.

p && q is used in C, C++, Java, JavaScript, and R.
p and q is used in Python, Ruby, and Pascal.
(and p q) is used in Lisp and Scheme.
p ∧ q in Agda

Note that these result in a truth value only, they do not hold on to any evidence.


In a computational judgment we need data (evidence) that proves the propositions. So a proposition \(P\) has data \(x\) that proves it, and a proposition \(Q\) has data \(y\) that proves it. We combine these as a joint proposition

(P,Q) in Scala
Pair<P,Q> in Java.
tuple[P,Q] in Python.
std::pair<P,Q> in C++.
P × Q in Agda.

These are just the propositions, they will need data to be proved.


In a practical judgment of a proposition \(P\) we associate some value \(\varepsilon\) of truth, for example, a percentage of our believe the \(P\) is true. If we have similar proposition \(Q\) with a value \(\delta\) then to judge \(P\wedge Q\) we need to combine these values. Some of the options include

min(ε,δ) assumes whichever the lower of two percentages should be the default.
ε*δ assumes the two percentages are independent and so the product is a reasonable estimate of the joint probability.




Introduction Rule for conjunction
Now get into what drives the meaning of “and” by describing what must be present to ensure we can create an instance of its use. Logicians call these introduction rules because they introduce the symbols of the logical operator, in this case \(\wedge\).

In natural language we use “and” when we combine two valid propositions \(P\) and \(Q\) to make a new valid proposition \(P\wedge Q\).
Now in symbolic language to say a proposition is valid is to have judged it in a context. So we start with \[
\Gamma \vdash P
\quad
\Delta \vdash Q
\] for contexts \(\Gamma\) and \(\Delta\). We conclude \[
\Gamma, \Delta \vdash P \wedge Q
\]

The mix of words and symbols is helpful initially but when we start to work with logic it becomes much more of a calculation, a calculus. Because this type of calculus is a movement of sequences it is known as sequent calculus. In the full sequent calculus we can collapse the words to this: \[
\tag{$I_{\wedge}$}
\begin{array}{rl}
    \Gamma &\vdash P\\
    \Delta & \vdash Q\\
\hline
    \Gamma, \Delta & \vdash P \wedge Q
\end{array}
\]

If we think of a program as making verified judgments then it makes sense that a proposition \(P\) has data \(x\) the proved it, and a proposition \(Q\) has data \(y\) that proved it. So to create data the proves both we can just hold on to both \(x\) and \(y\). The notation for this is an ordered pair \((x,y)\). The notations vary between programming languages, here are some popular options. Assuming x and y are already data:

p=(x,y) in Python, Ruby, and JavaScript.
(define p (list x y)) in Lisp and Scheme.
Pair p = new Pair(x,y) in Java.
p = <x,y> in Magma.
auto p = std::make_pair(x, y); in C++.




Elimination Rule for conjunction
Once we have conjoined two propositions we can carry them around as a single proposition until we intend to use it. It is at this point that we want the ability reach back and extract the to original propositions. Logicians call these elimination rules because they eliminate the symbols of the logical operator, in this case \(\wedge\). Something new happens with this step because it not one but two uses we expect. So technically we are after two elimination rules.

In natural language we use \(P\wedge Q\) so that we can know \(P\) or that we can know \(Q\), or both. So we need to change from a context that judged \(P\wedge Q\) to a context that judges \(P\) and a context that judges \(Q\). In symbolic language we can write this as two elimination rules: \[
\frac{
    \Gamma\vdash P\wedge Q
}{
    \Gamma \vdash P
}(E_{-\wedge *})
\qquad
\frac{
    \Gamma\vdash P\wedge Q
}{
    \Gamma \vdash Q
}(E_{*\wedge -})
\]

when we have a reason \(R\) to know of a proposition \(P\wedge Q\) given to us in a context \(\Gamma\). Then we can say that \(R\to P\) represents that the reason \(R\) leads to \(P\) and \(R\to Q\) represents that the reason \(R\) leads to \(Q\). In diagram language we could say \(R\to (P\wedge Q)\) represents that the reason \(R\) leads to both \(P\) and \(Q\).

Finally in symbolic language this would be the following rule to add to our proof tree options.


p[0] in Python, Ruby, and JavaScript.
(car p) for first, (cdr p) for rest, in Lisp and Scheme.
p.fst or x where t=(x y) in Haskell.

A diagram view of “And”
we can start to get more specific and insist that a contect \(\Gamma\) be given which judged \(P\) to be true.

\frac{
    \Gamma\vdash P,\qquad
    \Gamma\vdash Q
}{
    \Gamma, R \vdash P \wedge Q

\]
In diagram language we get much more precise and recognize a reason \(f\) the \(R\) leads to \(P\), written \(f:R\to P\). A possibly different reason \(g:R\to Q\) explains why \(R\) leads to \(Q\). The $ and \(R\to Q\) represents that the reason \(R\) leads to \(Q\). Then we can say that \(R\to (P\wedge Q)\) represents that the reason \(R\) leads to both \(P\) and \(Q\).

Now since a context can include any one of its propositions, it is common to simply absorb \(R\) into \(\Gamma\) and write \(\Gamma \vdash P\) and \(\Gamma \vdash Q\) as the premises of the rule and \(\Gamma \vdash P\wedge Q\) as the conclusion. In fact some authors will even fathom \(P\) and \(Q\) as coming initially from separate contexts \(\Gamma\) and \(\Delta\) and write the rule as \[
\frac{
    \Gamma\vdash P,\qquad
    \Delta\vdash Q
}{
    \Gamma, \Delta \vdash P \wedge Q
}
\] This not really more general and it disguises from discussion the implicit assumption that to speak of \(P\) and \(Q\) at the same times must occur from some common reason \(R\). By making the role of \(R\) explicit we can draw a more clear diagram of the process.

4.3 Clarity through Syntax
In order to be extra clear about our logic we want to set aside the words in natural language an use instead symbols or words in special fonts so as to treat the rules with some rigor that cannot miscommunicate out meaning. To so this we start to make a system that resembles arithmetic with is various additions, subtractions and other operators. When we calculate with any symbols we get what is known as a “Calculus”
So far we have seen \(\lambda\)-calculus and now we will be looking at two further Calculi, Propositional and Sequent. This is as good a place as any to pause and mention the list of “calculi” that exist in this course.
As a cultural warning, when some says they are studying “Calculus” chances are they mean one of the first two. Our main objective is to start making logical operators and we will focus on “AND”. In assignments you will explore “OR” and “NOT”

* Objectives

Identify Premise and Conclusion from a logical expression.
Use sequent calculus notation to write down logical operators such as AND, TRUE.
Demonstration the use of introduction and elimination rules.



*And by Sequent Calculus


Sequent calculus video
YouTube video player


Sequent Calculus Slides
Sequent Calculus


Sequents
Sequents means “parts of as a sequence” and the entire idea is to separate the premise from a conclusion. The devices to separate can just be a line, a long space, a word like “entails” but the most common one today is the turnstyle ⊢also said “vdash” since that is how you look it up as a font.
Sequents calculus is the use of sequence to calculate truth in a specified logic. If our logic only has “and” we can only calculate how make an and (introduction) and how to apply an and (elimination). All this must be written in a language.

(L)anguage : the alphabat, symbols, and grammar to be used in the sequents. If your sequents do not parse in the grammar then they don’t count.
(I)ntroduction : what premise or premises do you need to get ot use your logical operator?
(E)limination : what premises along with context do you need to use a logical operator?

The LIE components of a logical operator are a good way to remember the steps.


Semantics
There is another way we can describe logical operators that get closer to our appreciation of what our data means. For example, 12 is even and positive is true because each of “12 is even” and “12 is positive” are true. If this is all we care about we can ignore the precise form in which we get the facts and focus purely on the values. This is known as “Semantic” reasoning.
When it comes the semantics of AND we insist on one rule:
Only True AND True should be True 
However this still leaves us lots of room to explore meaning.

Classical Theoretical Logic
In classical logic, what experts call “KL” (the German initials) we insist every event is judged as true \(\top\) or false \(\bot\) with no middle values allowed (that rule is called the “Law of the Excluded Middle (LEM)”). That means that \(P\wedge Q\) can take only 4 combinations.








\(P\)
\(Q\)
\(P\wedge Q\)

\(\bot\)

\(\bot\)

\(\bot\)



Many times this information is recorded more compactly as a table where \(P\) and \(Q\) label the rows and columns
\[
\begin{array}{|c|cc|}
\hline
\wedge & \top & \bot \\
\hline
\top & \top & \bot \\
\bot & \bot & \bot\\
\hline
\end{array}
\] In fact when computing we often replace the symbols with 0 \(\bot\) and 1 \(\top\) and notice this is the multiplication rules of these numbers
\[
\begin{array}{|c|cc|}
\hline
* & 1 & 0 \\
\hline
1& 1 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0\\
\hline
\end{array}
\]
Notice we could be using very different algorithms to calculate AND through semantics. We might be looking things up in a table or multiplying integers, or using transistors in special configuration called a logic-gate. The point is, if we look at AND as is values instead of its syntax we have the freedom to engineer how we actually apply AND. That can be a powerful feature.


Many valued logical AND
Finally, much of life is not so certain and while we may describe some things as true \(\top\) we might struggle to conclude that all other things are false \(\bot\). For that many logics have been created that use further values. Sometimes it is a U for “Unknown”. Some times a “M” for mixed” (maybe a concept that has elements of truth and falsity), or “F(x)” for a “fuzzy truth $0x$” to measure quantities that vary continuously.
I like to use the symbol \(+\) because it seems typographically between \(\top\) and \(\bot\) and reminds me we could slide the bar up or down to introduce many subdivisions of “truth”. Obeying the rule of and: ONLY TRUE AND TRUE IS TRUE, we are still permitted to assign the remains values in different ways. For example, perhaps \(\top \wedge +\) should be \(+\), meaning, if you have something true and something partially true, then the whole thing is partially true. Of course context gets to decide what will count as the new meaning of AND. We close by detailing one of the ANDs as defined by the logician Kleene.
\[
\begin{array}{|c|ccc|}
\hline
\wedge & \top & + & \bot \\
\hline
\top & \top & + & \bot \\
+ & + & +  & \bot \\
\bot & \bot & \bot & \bot\\
\hline
\end{array}
\]
In words: truth and truth is true; truth and partial truth is partially true but any value and a falsity is false. There are clearly many ways that this captures the mode of a logic for AND even when we cannot be certain that our data is good enough to make things exactly true or false. And to make this semantics into arithmetic, suppose we used 1 for \(\top\), 0 for \(+\), and -1 of \(\bot\). Then \(P\wedge Q\) becomes merely \(\min(P,Q)\). For example \(\min(1,0)=0\) which is what it means to have True and Partially true being only Partially true.
As you develop your logic you may have many other ways to approach operators like this one. But resist the urge to call it an AND unless it obey the main rule: Only True and True is True.

text:
5.1 The Universal Quantifier \(\forall\)
Once more we can look to natural language to get a hint about what logical operators we will find useful. Think of giving out the same instruction to an ever growing list of employees:
There a number of disadvantages to this approach. For one thing we are letting natural language get away with some imprecise form. Notice there is only one use of the word AND yet the Language of AND works in pairs <this> AND <that>. So the proper form would need us to pair up the instructions for which we invent parentheses
Of course this is one of many ways we could pair up the AND’s without actually making the logic any easier to explain.
Since logic is invented by humans for human, it makes sense to create a version of AND which is much more forgiving about repeated use. This would allow us to get the idea into a precise language we could use in reasoning and making future programs. What should this “repeated AND” be called? Pause to think of how you might say the instructions in simpler way. Here are some options that come to my mind.
While the natural languages we use on each other have many choices for style and emphasis, we can see the basic form is not working to avoid listing all the people and instead index them into a single category “Employee”, state the rule they must obey “Wash hands” and then quantify who in the employee list has this requirement: ALL/EACH/EVERY.
The logical operator “For all” is denoted \(\forall\) as an upside-down letter “A” (for “All”). To express it we follow the L.I.E.

5  Quantifiers $\forall$, $\exists$, $=$, and $!^n$

title: 5  Quantifiers \(\forall\), \(\exists\), \(=\), and \(!^n\)
text:
Language of For All

The grammar of a universal quantifier is given by \[
\tag{$L_{\forall}$}
\langle universal\rangle ::= \forall \langle \text{variable}\rangle . \langle\text{Predicate}\rangle
\] In words we say “For all \(x\), \(P(x)\) is valid” where \(x\) is a variable and \(P(x)\) is a predicate. Variations include “\(P(x)\) holds, for all \(x\)” and “for every \(x\), \(P(x)\) is valid”.

Notice this is another example of binding a variable. So just as with substitution rules and the Paradox of the trapped variable, we need to be careful to rename \(x\) when substituting.

Proposition 1. \(\forall n.(n<n+1)\).
Here the variable is \(n\) and the predicate is \(n<n+1\).
It is not necessary that the predicate actually depend on the variable, for example
Proposition 2. \(\forall n. (2+2=4)\).



Elimination of For All
We have not forgotten how to spell LIE but we are skipping ahead to the elimination rule because this is what truly organizes what “for all” does. When the manager asserts that “All employees wash their hands!” the meaning is found by applying this claim to any single employee. For example this means “Brenda must wash her hands!” And a new employee “Henri must wash his hands!” Notice the application no longer features “All” nor a variable “employee”. Thus it is an elimination of the structure of the operator.

\[
\tag{$E_{\forall}$}
\begin{array}{rl} \Gamma & \vdash \forall x.P(x)\\ \Gamma & \vdash c \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash P(c)\end{array}
\]
In words:

If context \(\Gamma\) leads to “For all x, P(x) is valid” and context also leads to a value c for x, then P(c) must hold in \(\Gamma\).”




Introduction Rule for universal quantifiers
Now that we know how to use the “for all” operator we can guess what we need to know to discover an example of a “for all” operator. Basically we need to reverse what we want as a conclusion. We need to know that if context can make a constant value c for x lead to P(c) being valid, then context is saying P(x) is valid “for all x”. This is quite similar to turning a substitution into a function by function abstraction. The major difference is that instead of a function that output data we think of universal quantifiers and proving a proposition.

\[
\tag{$I_{\forall}$}
\begin{array}{rl} \Gamma, c & \vdash P(c) \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash \forall x.P(x)\end{array}
\]
In software, a universal quantifier uses a computational judgement, hence evidence (data) must be produced for each \(P(x)\). In other words \(\forall x.P(x)\) in a Brouwerian judgment is synonymous with a function \(x\mapsto P\).

Notice the premise now has an unknown constant c which together with context leads to P(c). How do we come up with that? We do that through a mix of assumption (hypothesis, axioms, laws) and proofs. For example, a manager or a health inspector make a rule that all employees must wash their hands. Can they really know that this has always been obeyed? Perhaps not but in theory that is how it should work. Once we begin to work in practice or in computation we might find we need to relax our rules. We saw this already with AND where we derived new logic based on include partial truths. We can do the same with “for all” but in order that we call something a “for all” we should keep at least on feature that the theory exhibits. And that is the elimination rule.
For example, if we relax to accept that perhaps some employee neglects to wash their hands we should be within our rights to fire the employee and the health inspector can close the restaurant. When it comes to “for all” it is must important to protect the outcome that clean hands handle food than it is to protect the way introduce the law.

text:
5.2 Existential Quantifier \(\exists\)

Language of existential quantifier

The grammar of an existential quantifier is given by \[
\tag{$L_{\exists}$}
\langle existential\rangle ::= \exists \langle \text{variable}\rangle . \langle\text{Predicate}\rangle
\] In words we say “There exists an \(x\) such that \(P(x)\) is valid” where \(x\) is a variable and \(P(x)\) is a predicate. Variations include “\(P(x)\) holds, for some \(x\)” and “there is at least one \(x\) such that \(P(x)\) is valid”.



Introduction rule for existential quantifiers

\[
\tag{$I_{\exists}$}
\begin{array}{rl} \Gamma & \vdash P(c) \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash \exists x.P(x)\end{array}
\]



Elimination rule for existential quantifiers

\[
\tag{$E_{\exists}$}
\begin{array}{rl} \Gamma & \vdash \exists x.P(x)\\ \Gamma, c & \vdash P(c) \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash Q\end{array}
\] In words:
> If context \(\Gamma\) leads to “There exists an x such that P(x) is valid” and context also leads to a value c for x, then P(c) must hold in \(\Gamma\) and hence Q must hold in \(\Gamma\).

text:
5.4 Counting quantifiers and uniqueness
In affine logic we remove the option to duplicate assumptions as this can related to physical resources. In the stricter linear logic we further require the use of every assumption.

$! x.P(x) $ means “there exists exactly one x such that P(x) is valid”. This is a counting quantifier. It can be expressed in terms of the existential and universal quantifiers as follows:


In a classical logic, the uniqueness quantifier can be expressed as follows: \[
\exists ! x.P(x) \equiv \exists x.(P(x) \wedge \forall y.(P(y) \Rightarrow x=y))
\] In words, “there exists exactly one \(x\) such that \(P(x)\) is valid” is equivalent to “there exists an \(x\) such that \(P(x)\) is valid and for all \(y\), if \(P(y)\) is valid then \(y\) must be equal to \(x\)”.


Linear and Affine Logics
Meanwhile a rule like contraction clearly seems suspect in concepts like “have a USB port” or “have an egg” where counting seems crucial for the logic. A logic that cares about such counting is often called a “linear logic” (if it needs an exact match) or an “affine logic” (if it is upper bounded by a count). You can find in programming languages like Idris and Rust that allow for these logics. They are especially useful when we care to track that all our files are and memory are used and released as expected, and to boost the security guarantees of vulnerable software. It is hard to ease drop on data if you can only read it once.

The following Idris code shows how to specify that a value can only be used once. Hence the following fails because it used the value hasUSB twice because the preceeding number 1 instruct Idris to use that value exactly once.
canKeyAndMouse : (1 hasUSB : PortScanner) -> Bool
canKeyAndMouse hasUSB = hasUSB && hasUSB 
It also fails if you do not use the value at all.
canKeyAndMouse : (1 hasUSB : PortScanner) 
                    -> Bool
canKeyAndMouse hasUSB = false 
Idris is only happy if you use the inputs exactly once, so you need to give it to options. Each gets used exactly once and captures the idea of our logic.
canKeyAndMouse : (1 hasUSB : PortScanner,
                  1 hasOtherUSB : PortScanner)
                  -> Bool
canKeyAndMouse hasUSB hasOtherUSB = 
                    hasUSB && hasOtherUSB


Rust makes a similar idea practical with ownership. A value once used transfer ownership and in effect disappears and cannot be reused. This is why the following could would fail.
let data = String::from("Pa$$w0rd");
send_to_captain(data);
// Next line causes error; data moved.
send_to_criminal(data); 
Here is a safe use of data.
let data = String::from("Pa$$w0rd");
send_to_captain(data);
// Next line causes error; data moved.
send_to_criminal(data); 
Unlike Idris, Rust does not require you to use the value.
let data = String::from("Pa$$w0rd");  
// data never used, but that's ok

Though nothing should stop you from learning languages like Idris and Rust, this article should convince you firstly of valuable uses for different than expected logic. When your situation demands you can involve future study and coding assistants to select the programming language that supports your logic best.

6.1 Math156 Dual logic and Programs
Is a good idea is worth repeating? Well in math and logic once we have solved a problem we don’t really need to solve it again. Rather what we mean in this situation is that we can repeat the spirit of the idea but with some useful changes. The variation we want to explore here are when the roles of the arrows are all reversed behavior can occur in reverse as well. Think of this as swapping inputs with outputs, saving a file verses reading a file, opening a window verses closing a window, and so on. When we do that we are in effect swapping the elimination rules with the introduction rules of some data types. With logic that means for example to swap AND with OR, True with False, and many similar so-called dualities. It is often a strong way to get a new functionality without much new work. But sometimes these dualities actually uncover missing parts of the original problem which help us make a better understanding of the entire logic.

* Fill-in-the-Blank
A function (f:XY) is bijective when for every (yY), (y=f(x)) has exactly one solution.


* Flashcards
Instructions - Injective
(f:XY) has a left inverse (f:YX^?) - Onto
Jargon for “Surjective” - One-to-one
Jargon for “Injective” - One-to-one correspondence
Jargon for “Bijective” - Bijective
(f:XY) has a two-sided inverse (f^{-1}:YX) - Surjective
(f:XY) has a right inverse (/f:YX) - Right invertible / “cancellable”
(uf=vf) leads to (u=v) - Left invertible / “cancellable”
(fu=fv) leads to (u=v) - (/f)
(f:XY), (/f:YX) where (xX. ((f/f)(x)=x)) - (f)
(f:XY), (f:YX) where (xX, ((ff)(x)=x)


What if your function is “none of the above”?
Pay attention that what is not being said is that (y=f(x)) sometimes have at least/at most/exactly one solution and sometimes not. Functions can have a mix of solution patterns but they only get the name surjective/injecitve/bijective when that pattern applies to all (yY). This means there are many functions that are none of the above. However, an important and crucial theorem of function is that they always factor into this pattern.
Theorem. Every function (f:XY) is the composition (f=ibc) where

(i) is injective and we call it the “image of (f)”,
(b) is bijective, and
(c) is surjective and we call the “co-image of (f)”.

Perhaps it is better to see this with an example. Imagine we think of customers ordering off of a menu in the morning. Not everything on the menu will be ordered. And items that sell can be said to have appealed to clients who have similar taste profiles. So we can break down the ordering process into 3 stages



Flow chart of customer ordering off of a menu as related to their profile and items sold.



Stage 1: Customer taste profiles (e.g. sweet tooth, picky eater, diet conscious, ….)
Stage 2: Match menu selection to each profile.
Stage 3: The sold item must all appear somewhere on the menu

This decomposition over simplifies the real life, for example even a regular customer profile can surprise us with a new order every now and then. But we take this theoretical observation more seriously by thinking of these functions as described in practical logics which allow for occasional inconsistencies. The field of Machine Learning is dedicated to tools that construct such functions as reasonably accurate approximations of customer profiles and their most likely menu choices.
What we do with the data after is still open to creativity. Perhaps we lower food costs by making our menu a closer to match to items that sell. Or perhaps we market to new customers increase the profile and sell more high-priced items from the menu. The math is here to do the job of point out how the data moves and to do so in regular predictable ways for which we can solve. You and your users get to imagine what becomes possible because of the math.

(W 15 mins) Bijective
Now lets us consider the most reversible of all functions, the bijective functions. These are when f(x)=bf(x)=b has exactly one solution. It is extremely rare, and, I will argue, comes about only when you are basically describing an alphabet for some data. Let us see what that means.

*Objectives

Define bijective.
Identify bijective with the existence of two-sided inverse.
Understand that 2-sided inverses are unique.
Demonstrate that bijections occur when two sets have the same size “cardinality”.



*Lectures
YouTube video player
In summary here is what we learn. A function (f:AB) is bijective precisely when one of the following is true.

For every (b:B), there is exactly one solution (x:A) to the equation (f(x)=b).
There is a function (f^{-1}:BA) such that (ff^{-1}(b)=b) and (f^{-1}f(a)=a).

Bijections line up every input with one output and vice-versa, which means that we can see the value in B as names for the inputs. If B were numbers, 1, 2,3,… it would be like we count off the value of A. But numbers often have extra properties like order and arithmetic. So a better mental model is to think of B as an alphabet, a,b,c,d,… possibly in a different language or with repeats such as (b_1,b_2,b_3,). In this way a bijection is like assigning characters from an alphabet to each of your inputs.
When we think of inputs and outputs as sets in the mathematical sense where there is a notion of size then a bijection just means |A|=|B|.


* Quick Check
There is a bijection between the lower-case and upper-case letters of the English language.
Yes
Exactly, the forward direction is to send lower-case to upper case and inverse is to send upper-case to lower-case.
No
While the sets are not the same, a bijection can exist that relates them to each other. Think of turning lower-case into upper-case.
Check Answer


* Quick Check
There is a bijection between even and odd integers.
Yes
Surprisingly yes. Take 2n to 2n-1. That will turn even to odd. And it has an inverse: send 2n-1 to 2n.
No

Week 7 Day 1: Relations and Orders
Day 1 Relations and Orders
We saw with deduction that one of the ways to build a new data type is to modify what we mean by “equals”. In programs we override equality. But you are likely familiar with other ways we relate data. For example, some numbers are large, others are small, that means (xy). Likewise some expressions in reasoning benefit from organization.

General Relations
To turn data like 541 or a PDF into a value we can judge we need to create a relation. Here are some samples relations.

P(541) = “541 is positive”. Something we can judge, and we judge it is true.
P(541) = “541 is even.” Something we can also judge, but this time we judge it is false.
Q(MyCV.pdf) = “MyCV.pdf has page numbers.” Something we can judge. Is it true? We’d have to read the file to find out.


Propositions
A Proposition is a sentence we can claim and judge. The outcome depends on our mode. Recall from Week 1 we have three forms of propositions

() for Theory is generally True () and False ()
() for Computation is generally True () and False () but must be supported by evidence so it may not come to an end if the evidence never comes.
() for Practice is generally True (), False () along with a host of gray are, perhaps Maybe, or Unknown, or Likely, Unlikely, etc. We will here simplify and just allow a single third value +.



Relations
So what is a Relation? First choose the appropriate proposition category (Theory, Computation, or Practice). Then a Relation is a function form lists of types (X_1, X_2,, X_n) into (). That is
(P:X_1X_n)

P(x) = “x is positive”. This is not something we can judge yet, but as soon as we replace the variable by a value we will be able to judge it. In fact this sort of claim is simply true of false, Theory proposition applies.. So this is a function from data into propositions but it only makes sense when given decimal numbers (). It is a Relation (P:{,})
P(x,y) = “x +y =0”. This is a either true or false, so we can judge this once given decimal numbers of x and y so this is a relation (P:{,})
Q(x) = “x has page numbers”. Here x is a file, so File is our input type. However, the concept of “has page number” is clear for documents but it means nothing for images, videos and so many other documents. This suggests a practical proposition of Prop={true, false, undefined}. This is a relation (Q: -> {}). In common software syntax this might be def hasPageNumbers(x : File) : Option[Boolean]. The Option wrapper allows us to give back a value of True/False when it makes sense, or nothing when the input file is not a document.



General Relation Vocabulary

Valence or Arity is the number of inputs to a relation. E.g. P(x), Q(x) are valence 1, also called unary. P(x,y) is binary, valence 2.
Homogeneous: a relation (R:X_1X_n) where for each (i,j), (X_i=X_j). In this case we often write (R:X^n).
Heterogenous: a relation that may not be homogeneous. In general a homogeneous relation is also heterogenous but not the other way around.

Mathematical Conventions
Mathematics tends to study relations (R:X_1X_n) more fully than other subjects and much of mathematics is in the Theory camp of reasoning. Because of this most of mathematics sees relations as just true and false. When this is the case then it is enough to know just the values which are true.
({(x_1,, x_n)X_1X_n R(x_1,, x_n) })
Because of this, much of mathematics will define relations not by a function but by a subset, that is, mathematics will often write
(RX_1X_n)
Even if this is bit short cited on the part of mathematicians not to consider the nuance of relations in computation and in practice, it is still a notation used broadly and you can introduce that notation meaning in fact (R:X_1X_n). Just add that clarity to your discussion in text.



Binary Homogeneous Relations
Amongst the most used relations are binary homogeneous relations
(R:XX)
In this case we generally prefer an infix notation. Example, instead of (R(x,y)) we choose some symbol, maybe = or < or == etc. and write things like
(x=y), (x<y), x==y, x!=y, (xy)
Since we need to keep talking about many binary homogeneous relations we will continue to use R as a generic name
(xRy)

Reflexive law
A binary homogeneous relation (R:X^2) is called reflexive if
(x.(xRx))

In number equality is reflexive (x=x), less than is not reflexive (5<5) is false, but less-than or equal is reflexive (xx)
In programming if one data type B extends another A it means every method for A is a method for B as well, though B may have further methods. Under this definition A has all the methods that A has so A extends A. However, in writing a program you may not be allowed to write A extends A as that leads the programming language to get confused with circular reasoning. This is a difference in definitions, so even experts can disagree on this one with good reason.
A daughter inherits traits from her father, but a daughter does not inherit traits from herself. So inheritence is not generally reflexive.

Reflexive Closure
In some situations it is convenient to assume a relation is reflexive even if it is not. Think of promoting (x<y) into (xy). This literally means
(xy := (x=x) (x<y))
We can do this to absolutely any binary homogeneous relation (R:X^2)
(xy := (x=x) (x<y))
The resulting relation (R^=) is called the reflexive closure. The notation we usually use is to add part of the equal sign to the original symbol. Here are some examples

(< )
()

In other situations we want to remove reflexivity. We can do this as well.
(xy := (xx) (xy))
The notation similarly strikes out the equal portion.


Transitive Law
So what makes something an order? While humans make the rules, and thus can change them, by far the most popular definitions agree on one rule, the transitive law.
( (a < b )(b< c) (a< c))


Symmetric and Anti-symmetric laws
Two further relations laws are commonly encountered.

Symmetric: (xRy yR x)
Anti-symmetric: (xRy yRx x=y)

As we have seen there is a notion of “closure” for each of these. We simply force a relation to be symmetric. However, the closure for anti-symmetric is more sublte because it is forced to change the notion of equality. So this creates what we early called a partition.



Special Relations
Now mostly because of the popular use there are a bunch of combinations of these four rules that get names and you might be expected to know them in your future so we lets give them here.

Equivalence relation
Definition. A homogeneous binary relation (R:X^2) is called an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, transitive, and symmetric.
Equivalence relations usually uses language like this
(x=y), (xy), (xy), x==y, x.equals(y), equals(x,y)
You may also here the words “congruent” or “equivalent” or “isomorphic” as synonyms to equivalence relations. As always, it is ok to ask someone to explain their terms if you are not sure what they mean. And if you use a term, be able to explain it yourself.


Order relations
Definition. A homogeneous binary relation (R:X^2) is called an order relation if it is transitive. It is furthermore

A pre order if it is transitive and reflexive
A partial order if it is transitive, reflexive, and anti-symmetric.
A total order if it is transitive, reflexive, anti-symmetric, and for every (x,yX), (xRy) or (yRx).

There are many traditional order languages but some common ones include
(x< y), (xy), (xy), (xy)
One of the reasons that transitive is so hard to avoid is that in almost all logics, entailment itself is transitive:
\[\begin{array}{rl}
P & \vdash Q\\
Q & \vdash R\\
\hline
P & \vdash R
\end{array}\]
So once we get going with propositions it is often hard to avoid the transitive condition.

title: 16  Week 8 Day 1 Should you Modify your Priors or Your Reasoning
text:
Day 1: Should you Modify your Priors or Your Reasoning
When you make a mistake you typically have one of two reactions:

Find out what you did wrong.
Figure out what you will do next.

These two strategies of often intermingled but they point to two largely distinct strategies for problem solving.

Default Reasoning.**
If you can understand what went wrong you might be able to fix it by introducing a modification to your original reasoning. You in effect had default assumption that turned out to be defeated by later evidence. By going back to that default you reset you prior understanding and move forward with a new default position.
In computation this might be something like assuming that the data set you loaded had been sorted alphabetically because all other examples had been sorted. But then you run across one data set that is not sorted. It defeats your default hypothesis. You then go back to your instructions for handling the data and look for what instructions should be made for unsorted data. Perhaps you first sort it, or perhaps you are instructed to removed it form the study. The point is, you located the source of the error and can now behave rationally form there.


Adaptive Reasoning.**
Meanwhile in the “figure out what to do next” camp, it may not be important to know how you go where you are, but you sure need a plan to get through the error. Imagine you’re running an app on your phone and it suddenly freezes. You may have no idea what strange combination of events occurred to make it freeze. It might be impossible to retrace your steps precisely enough to ever reproduce the bug. But it’s typically not that important to solve the source of the puzzle because you might just close the app and restart it to find it now works. It is a messy alternative to problem solving because we might loose some work we already did but it is far less time to reenter some values than it would be to do a detailed study of what triggered the bug.
This is a situation that calls for “Adaptive Logic”. Loosely speaking we run two logics. A lower logic that has a set of very realistic properties such as assumptions that data can be contradictory, resources limited, power to code go out etc. This lower logic is pessimistic and difficult to use for most natural projects so then we install an Upper Logic with convenient properties like “programs never freeze” “you have all the resources you need” and so on. The lower logic runs the Upper Logic almost like a video game runs on a computer or an webpage runs in a browser. It is simulating an environment that is well behaved. But should a problem actually occur, the lower logic is there to step in, close the app, reset, and start over.


Inconsistent reasoning and how to make it consistent
Before doing a deeper dive into the precise mechanics of default and adaptive logic it will help us to consider first how it is that we represent mistakes, bugs, and other inconsistent events in logic. That will make it much more obvious what are the strategies to begin fixing them. Chief amongst the strategies is to realize that mistakes/bugs/inconsistences are always a matter of perspective. They do of course actually happen. Which proves they are in fact “logical”. They only appear “illogical” because we lack the right context when we first an approach the question. So lets revisit context as means to identify inconsistency in a logically sound manner.

Classical Inconsistency
In classical logic, the type of logic we often us in theory, we want avoid a situation where everything is true. This may seem a strange way to define inconsistency but imagine if everything is true then what would be the point of any reasoning? One way we can state this is by insisting on at least one false assumption.


Non-monotone logic
Lets revisit validity to see a nuance that we never settled but which probably was filled in with a default assumption which now we need to correct.
Recall that we write (AB) we are saying that (A)leads to, validates,(B)
Example.If I see the symbol 📶 then I can browse the web on my phone.

A = “I see the symbol 📶”
B = “browse the web on my phone”
(A)

However we have all of us experienced a situation where the icons are misleading and although we have a signal we somehow cannot get through. So here is an expanded scenario.
Ex.If I see the symbol 📶 then I can browse the web on my phone.But often when I land after a flight in a new time zone my phone can’t locate my carrier so it doesn’t work to browse after all.

A = “I see the symbol 📶”
B = “browse the web on my phone”
(AB)
C = “New time zone”
(C,A B)

This is a demonstration that logical reasoning is quite oftennon-monotonic
DefinitionA system of logic ismonotoneif whenever (AB) then (C,AB). If this is not always the case then we call the logicnon-monotonic.
Whether a logic is monotone or non-monotone has all the usual divisions of being a mix of Theoretical, Computational, and Practical. It is not about contradictions or the meaning of truth vs. evidence. It is about whether we insist that validity always builds up (monotone) or if validity can be “defeated” by future evidence. In the phone example it was logical to read (AB) in fact this is what the design of the phone says is the point of the icon. But it is also logical to defeat that logic when further evidence gives a broader context that explains exceptions to that behavior.
The point of non-monotonic logic is to offer scaffolding to work through scenarios where non-monotonic reasoning is required and select the desired behavior. Often these situations are left unresolved or left to individual programers to select a solution based on whim or instinct rather than optimal behavior.
The world of default and adaptive logic are filled with algorithms and strategies that optimize against desired cost functions (e.g. make the most people happy). A main objective to make students aware that there is an entire body of algorithms and known limits to exception handling and often the ad hoc solutions are suboptimal.

Day 1: Proportions towards Probability
Abductive reasoning is when we have a context () (which might include some known facts and theories) and an observed result (R) and we must try to solve for a hypothesis (H) such that
(,HR)
For example, in the following image of a car accident, the car on the left has its front bumper pressed against the side door of the car on the right. This would be the result (R) of the accident. The context () would be driving rules and conditions. A plausible hypothesis (H) is that the left car hit the right car. This does not dismiss the possibility of a more complex hypothesis (K) where the right care slide into the left car. We would need to investigate for further parts of the result (R) such as slick conditions, or witnesses. But given the scenario just described the hypothesis (K) ranks as “less likely” than (H).



A car accident with the left car’s hood touching the right car’s side door.



Probability as Quantitative Abductive Logic
The challenge to rank events (KH) is the opening we need to add mathematics to the art of abductive logic. Let us add some further conditions on this ranking which we denote (Prob(X)) of an event (X).

The ranking should be a total order, that is,
Transitive: if we rank (X) as less likely than (Y), i.e. (Prob(X)< Prob(Y)) and (Y) as less likely than (Z), i.e. (Prob(Y)Prob(Z)) then we can conclude that (X) is less likely than (Z), i.e. (Prob(X)Prob(Z)).
Total: Any two ranked events should be comparable, so (Prob(X)Prob(Y)) or (Prob(Y)Prob(X)).
Reflexive. Events are as likely as themselves (Prob(X)Prob(X)).
Anti-symmetric: If events that out rank each other are in fact equally likely: (Prob(X)Prob(Y)) and (Prob(Y)Prob(X)) leads to (Prob(X)=Prob(Y)).
A bottom rank. The absence of an event has a measure, typically denoted by 0, so (Prob()=0)
A top rank. The measure of all events, denoted () has a maximum measure typically denoted 1, so (Prob()=1).

It turns out that the decimal numbers ([0,1]={x x}) satisfy exactly these rules. So over the past 150 years scientist have been developing a specific plan to quantify some forms of abductive logic by insisting on a function (Prob(X)) as a decimal number between 0 and 1. Its starting point is probably something you already know.


Proportions as a first Probability
Imagine you fill a bag with red and blue balls. (In probability circles it is typical to use an urn instead of a bag.). You reach into the bag and pull out a ball. What color do you expect to see? It is hard to say. But suppose I now tell you there are 30 red balls and 10 blue. You probably expect to see a red ball as your first choice. What if I change the that 25 red and 15 blue? You might still favor red but less than before. How about 21 red and 19 blue? You might now start to return to the uncertainty of expecting red or blue.
What this thought experiment illustrates is that much of our abductive reasoning can be quantified using proportions.

There 10/40 blue vs. 30/40 red suggests red is more plausible than blue just as 10/40 < 30/40.
There 15/40 blue vs. 25/40 red suggests red is more plausible than blue just as 15/40 < 25/40, but our certainty dropped because 25/40 < 30/40.
There 19/40 blue vs. 21/40 red suggests red is just slightly more plausible than blue just as 19/40 = 0.475 < 0.525 = 21/40 but not by much.

A proportion of a set of events (X) is its size divided by the size of all events ()
(Proportion(X) := )
In this story an event is a single ball being chosen. So (X)= “a red ball is chosen” is an event with 30 options in the first case, 25 in the second, and 21 in the last. Proportions are by design always between 0 and 1. A 0 proportion occurs when no events occur and a 1 when all events occur. And we can compare any subset of events in this way because any two subsets (X,Y) have a finite size.
Proportions are the first and main example of a probability, that is, an assignment of a number to an abductive reasoning problem. Let us set up the details.

Context (): Drawing balls from a bag with red and blue balls.
Result : (R) draw a red.
First Hypothesis: (H) There are more red balls than blue balls.
Second Hypothesis :(K) Random event.

If we look at this scenario we cannot resolve if one draw suggests one hypothesis is better than another. But if we repeat the experiment (always returning the ball we choose to the bag and we find after 4 trials

Result: Red, Red, Blue, Red

We could perhaps now have some support for the first hypothesis and we could explain it as the expected values of 3/4 red, 1/4 blue proportion of balls. We still could not truly know unless we list all the balls. There may not be enough time to do such a lengthy count. So instead we take our proportion as evidence of some form of growing belief that there may be more red than blue balls and our confidence in this has something to do with the numbers 3/4 and 1/4.
